claim: Channelrhodopsin has been widely used to study and manipulate neuronal activity in vivo.
source: The light-gated Channelrhodopsin has been widely used to study and manipulate neuronal activity in vivo, whereas optogenetic control of second messengers in vivo has not been examined in depth.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the abstract without specific data or citations in this sentence.

claim: Optogenetic control of second messengers in vivo has not been examined in depth.
source: The light-gated Channelrhodopsin has been widely used to study and manipulate neuronal activity in vivo, whereas optogenetic control of second messengers in vivo has not been examined in depth.
evidence: This is stated as a gap in current knowledge in the abstract.

claim: A transgenic mouse model expressing photoactivated adenylyl cyclase (bPAC) in sperm has been created.
source: In this study, we present a transgenic mouse model expressing a photoactivated adenylyl cyclase (bPAC) in sperm.
evidence: The creation of the transgenic mouse model is described in the abstract and detailed in the Results section with supporting figures.

claim: In transgenic sperm, bPAC mimics the action of the endogenous soluble adenylyl cyclase (SACY) that is required for motility and fertilization.
source: In transgenic sperm, bPAC mimics the action of the endogenous soluble adenylyl cyclase (SACY) that is required for motility and fertilization: light-stimulation rapidly elevates cAMP, accelerates the flagellar beat, and, thereby, changes swimming behavior of sperm.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figures 2 and 4 showing cAMP elevation and motility changes.

claim: Light-stimulation of bPAC rapidly elevates cAMP in sperm.
source: In transgenic sperm, bPAC mimics the action of the endogenous soluble adenylyl cyclase (SACY) that is required for motility and fertilization: light-stimulation rapidly elevates cAMP, accelerates the flagellar beat, and, thereby, changes swimming behavior of sperm.
evidence: This is directly supported by cAMP measurements shown in Figure 2A and 2B.

claim: Light-stimulation of bPAC accelerates the flagellar beat in sperm.
source: In transgenic sperm, bPAC mimics the action of the endogenous soluble adenylyl cyclase (SACY) that is required for motility and fertilization: light-stimulation rapidly elevates cAMP, accelerates the flagellar beat, and, thereby, changes swimming behavior of sperm.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figure 2H-K showing beat frequency changes.

claim: Light-stimulation of bPAC changes swimming behavior of sperm.
source: In transgenic sperm, bPAC mimics the action of the endogenous soluble adenylyl cyclase (SACY) that is required for motility and fertilization: light-stimulation rapidly elevates cAMP, accelerates the flagellar beat, and, thereby, changes swimming behavior of sperm.
evidence: This is supported by videos and motility analysis presented in the Results section.

claim: bPAC replaces endogenous adenylyl cyclase activity in mutant sperm lacking bicarbonate-stimulated SACY activity.
source: Furthermore, bPAC replaces endogenous adenylyl cyclase activity. In mutant sperm lacking the bicarbonate-stimulated SACY activity, bPAC restored motility after light-stimulation and, thereby, enabled sperm to fertilize oocytes in vitro.
evidence: This is demonstrated by experiments with Slc9a10-null/bPAC sperm shown in Figure 4.

claim: bPAC restored motility after light-stimulation in mutant sperm lacking bicarbonate-stimulated SACY activity.
source: In mutant sperm lacking the bicarbonate-stimulated SACY activity, bPAC restored motility after light-stimulation and, thereby, enabled sperm to fertilize oocytes in vitro.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4C and Video 5.

claim: bPAC enabled mutant sperm lacking bicarbonate-stimulated SACY activity to fertilize oocytes in vitro.
source: In mutant sperm lacking the bicarbonate-stimulated SACY activity, bPAC restored motility after light-stimulation and, thereby, enabled sperm to fertilize oocytes in vitro.
evidence: This is demonstrated by in vitro fertilization data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Almost every eukaryotic cell contains a specialized surface protrusion called the primary cilium.
source: Almost every eukaryotic cell contains a specialized surface protrusion called the primary cilium (Singla and Reiter, 2006).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Singla and Reiter, 2006.

claim: Primary cilia serve as sensory antennae that register physical and chemical cues from the environment.
source: Primary cilia serve as sensory antennae that register physical and chemical cues from the environment.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the Introduction.

claim: Cilia are involved in mechano-, chemo-, and photo-sensation.
source: Cilia are not only involved in for example, mechano-, chemo-, and photo-sensation but also in embryonic and neuronal development (Praetorius and Spring 2001; Singla and Reiter, 2006; Insinna and Besharse, 2008; Goetz and Anderson, 2010; Satir et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Cilia are involved in embryonic and neuronal development.
source: Cilia are not only involved in for example, mechano-, chemo-, and photo-sensation but also in embryonic and neuronal development (Praetorius and Spring 2001; Singla and Reiter, 2006; Insinna and Besharse, 2008; Goetz and Anderson, 2010; Satir et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Motile cilia are used both as sensory antenna and motors that move fluids or propel cells.
source: Motile cilia, also called flagella, are used both as sensory antenna and motors that move fluids or propel cells (Salathe, 2007; Bloodgood, 2010; Lindemann and Lesich, 2010; Pichlo et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Signaling in cilia and flagella is tightly regulated, spatially confined, and relies on a cilia-specific transport machinery.
source: Signaling in cilia and flagella is tightly regulated, spatially confined, and relies on a cilia-specific transport machinery (Rosenbaum and Witman, 2002; Delling et al., 2013; Chung et al., 2014; Pichlo et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Cyclic nucleotide-dependent signaling plays a central role in both primary and motile cilia.
source: Cyclic nucleotide-dependent signaling plays a central role in both primary and motile cilia.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge and supported by subsequent citations.

claim: In ciliary structures of olfactory neurons and photoreceptors, cyclic nucleotide signaling regulates chemosensation and photoreception, respectively.
source: In ciliary structures of olfactory neurons and photoreceptors, it regulates chemosensation and photoreception, respectively (Johnson and Leroux, 2010).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Johnson and Leroux, 2010.

claim: In cilia of endothelial and mesenchymal cells, cAMP signaling controls cilia length in response to extracellular stimuli.
source: In cilia of endothelial and mesenchymal cells, cAMP signaling controls cilia length in response to extracellular stimuli (Besschetnova et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Besschetnova et al., 2010.

claim: Defects in cilia of the renal epithelium cause polycystic kidney disease.
source: Defects in cilia of the renal epithelium cause polycystic kidney disease (Pazour et al., 2000).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Pazour et al., 2000.

claim: During embryonic development, ciliary cAMP signaling is involved in neural tube development by regulating the Sonic hedgehog (Shh) pathway.
source: During embryonic development, ciliary cAMP signaling is involved in neural tube development by regulating the Sonic hedgehog (Shh) pathway (Mukhopadhyay et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Mukhopadhyay et al., 2013.

claim: Cyclic AMP signaling is essential for sperm development, motility, and maturation in the female genital tract.
source: Cyclic AMP signaling is essential for sperm development, motility, and maturation in the female genital tract (Visconti et al., 1995b; Wennemuth et al., 2003; Krähling et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: CRIS, a cAMP-binding protein, controls spermatogenesis and sperm motility.
source: CRIS, a cAMP-binding protein, controls spermatogenesis and sperm motility (Krähling et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Krähling et al., 2013.

claim: An increase in bicarbonate during the transit from the epididymis to the female genital tract activates a soluble adenylyl cyclase (SACY).
source: An increase in bicarbonate (HCO3−) during the transit from the epididymis to the female genital tract activates a soluble adenylyl cyclase (SACY) and, thereby, accelerates the flagellar beat and enhances progressive sperm motility (Esposito et al., 2004; Xie et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Esposito et al., 2004 and Xie et al., 2006.

claim: Activation of SACY by bicarbonate accelerates the flagellar beat and enhances progressive sperm motility.
source: An increase in bicarbonate (HCO3−) during the transit from the epididymis to the female genital tract activates a soluble adenylyl cyclase (SACY) and, thereby, accelerates the flagellar beat and enhances progressive sperm motility (Esposito et al., 2004; Xie et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Esposito et al., 2004 and Xie et al., 2006.

claim: HCO3−-induced cAMP synthesis by SACY stimulates protein kinase A (PKA).
source: HCO3−-induced cAMP synthesis by SACY stimulates protein kinase A (PKA) (Wennemuth et al., 2003; Nolan et al., 2004) and controls capacitation, a maturation process of sperm in the female genital tract that is essential for fertilization (Chang, 1951; Austin, 1952).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Wennemuth et al., 2003 and Nolan et al., 2004.

claim: SACY controls capacitation, a maturation process of sperm in the female genital tract that is essential for fertilization.
source: HCO3−-induced cAMP synthesis by SACY stimulates protein kinase A (PKA) (Wennemuth et al., 2003; Nolan et al., 2004) and controls capacitation, a maturation process of sperm in the female genital tract that is essential for fertilization (Chang, 1951; Austin, 1952).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Chang, 1951 and Austin, 1952.

claim: The beat frequency increases within seconds after HCO3− stimulation.
source: Acceleration of the flagellar beat and capacitation proceed on quite different time scales: the beat frequency increases within seconds, whereas PKA-dependent tyrosine phosphorylation, a hallmark of sperm capacitation, takes about an hour to become noticeable (Visconti et al., 1995a).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge and supported by a citation.

claim: PKA-dependent tyrosine phosphorylation, a hallmark of sperm capacitation, takes about an hour to become noticeable.
source: Acceleration of the flagellar beat and capacitation proceed on quite different time scales: the beat frequency increases within seconds, whereas PKA-dependent tyrosine phosphorylation, a hallmark of sperm capacitation, takes about an hour to become noticeable (Visconti et al., 1995a).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Visconti et al., 1995a.

claim: Ca2+ controls SACY activity.
source: The study of cAMP-dependent signaling pathways in mammalian sperm is further complicated by an ill-defined interplay between cAMP and Ca2+ signaling; for example, Ca2+ controls SACY activity (Carlson et al., 2007) and cAMP reportedly evokes a Ca2+ influx (Kobori et al., 2000; Ren et al., 2001; Xia et al., 2007; Wertheimer et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Carlson et al., 2007.

claim: cAMP reportedly evokes a Ca2+ influx in sperm.
source: The study of cAMP-dependent signaling pathways in mammalian sperm is further complicated by an ill-defined interplay between cAMP and Ca2+ signaling; for example, Ca2+ controls SACY activity (Carlson et al., 2007) and cAMP reportedly evokes a Ca2+ influx (Kobori et al., 2000; Ren et al., 2001; Xia et al., 2007; Wertheimer et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Kobori et al., 2000; Ren et al., 2001; Xia et al., 2007; Wertheimer et al., 2013.

claim: Recent studies in human sperm refute that cAMP controls [Ca2+]i.
source: Recent studies in human sperm, however, refute that cAMP controls [Ca2+]i (Strünker et al., 2011) and disclose serious shortcomings of these pharmacological tools that directly act on the sperm Ca2+ channel CatSper and, thereby, artifactually change Ca2+ levels (Brenker et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Strünker et al., 2011.

claim: Pharmacological tools used to study cAMP signaling have serious shortcomings as they directly act on the sperm Ca2+ channel CatSper and artifactually change Ca2+ levels.
source: Recent studies in human sperm, however, refute that cAMP controls [Ca2+]i (Strünker et al., 2011) and disclose serious shortcomings of these pharmacological tools that directly act on the sperm Ca2+ channel CatSper and, thereby, artifactually change Ca2+ levels (Brenker et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Brenker et al., 2012.

claim: The bPAC cDNA sequence was modified for expression in mammalian systems according to Stierl et al. (2011).
source: The bPAC cDNA (beta subunit of photo-activated adenylyl cyclase from Beggiatoa sp. PS, BGP_1043; modified for expression in mammalian systems according to Stierl et al. (2011), GU461307) sequence was amplified via PCR.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Stierl et al., 2011.

claim: The protamine 1 promoter is exclusively active in post-meiotic spermatids.
source: We engineered a targeting vector to express the beta subunit of photo activated adenylyl cyclase from the soil bacterium Beggiatoa (bPAC) under the control of the protamine 1 promoter (Prm1, Figure 1A) that is exclusively active in post-meiotic spermatids (Zambrowicz et al., 1993).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Zambrowicz et al., 1993.

claim: Genomic insertion of the transgene was confirmed by PCR.
source: Genomic insertion of the transgene was confirmed by PCR (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Protein expression of bPAC in testis lysates varied between different founder lines.
source: Protein expression of bPAC in testis lysates varied between different founder lines (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Variation in transgene expression reflects differences in integration site and/or copy number.
source: This variation in transgene expression reflects differences in integration site and/or copy number.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation of variable expression between founder lines.

claim: The bPAC protein was exclusively expressed in sperm.
source: The bPAC protein was exclusively expressed in sperm (Figure 1D–F).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot and immunohistochemistry data shown in Figures 1D-F.

claim: Prm1-bPAC males were fertile.
source: Prm1-bPAC males were fertile and did not show any defects during spermatogenesis, demonstrating that bPAC expression does not affect sperm development or function (Figure 1—source data 1).
evidence: This is supported by fertility data referenced in Figure 1—source data 1.

claim: Prm1-bPAC males did not show any defects during spermatogenesis.
source: Prm1-bPAC males were fertile and did not show any defects during spermatogenesis, demonstrating that bPAC expression does not affect sperm development or function (Figure 1—source data 1).
evidence: This is supported by data referenced in Figure 1—source data 1.

claim: bPAC expression does not affect sperm development or function.
source: Prm1-bPAC males were fertile and did not show any defects during spermatogenesis, demonstrating that bPAC expression does not affect sperm development or function (Figure 1—source data 1).
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that Prm1-bPAC males were fertile and showed no spermatogenesis defects.

claim: Basal cAMP levels in bPAC sperm were slightly enhanced compared to wild-type sperm.
source: Basal cAMP levels in bPAC sperm were slightly enhanced (bPAC: 15.3 ± 3.6 fmol/105 sperm versus wild-type: 10.0 ± 4.4 fmol/105 sperm; Figure 2A), which might be due to basal bPAC activity (Stierl et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by cAMP measurements shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The enhanced basal cAMP levels in bPAC sperm might be due to basal bPAC activity.
source: Basal cAMP levels in bPAC sperm were slightly enhanced (bPAC: 15.3 ± 3.6 fmol/105 sperm versus wild-type: 10.0 ± 4.4 fmol/105 sperm; Figure 2A), which might be due to basal bPAC activity (Stierl et al., 2011).
evidence: This is speculative reasoning supported by a citation to Stierl et al., 2011.

claim: In wild-type sperm, light stimulation did not alter cAMP levels.
source: In wild-type sperm, light stimulation did not alter cAMP levels, whereas in bPAC sperm, cAMP levels increased by about 2.5-fold (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is supported by cAMP measurements shown in Figure 2A.

claim: In bPAC sperm, light stimulation increased cAMP levels by about 2.5-fold.
source: In wild-type sperm, light stimulation did not alter cAMP levels, whereas in bPAC sperm, cAMP levels increased by about 2.5-fold (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is supported by cAMP measurements shown in Figure 2A.

claim: During continuous light stimulation, cAMP levels reached a maximum within 2 min.
source: During continuous light stimulation, cAMP levels reached a maximum within 2 min (Figure 2B); after switching off the light, cAMP returned to baseline within 10 min (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is supported by time-course cAMP measurements shown in Figure 2B.

claim: After switching off the light, cAMP returned to baseline within 10 min.
source: During continuous light stimulation, cAMP levels reached a maximum within 2 min (Figure 2B); after switching off the light, cAMP returned to baseline within 10 min (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is supported by time-course cAMP measurements shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The light-induced cAMP increase was similar to the HCO3−-induced cAMP increase.
source: The light-induced cAMP increase was similar to the HCO3−-induced cAMP increase (Figure 2A), indicating that activation of bPAC mimics the activation of SACY by HCO3−.
evidence: This is supported by comparative cAMP measurements shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Activation of bPAC mimics the activation of SACY by HCO3−.
source: The light-induced cAMP increase was similar to the HCO3−-induced cAMP increase (Figure 2A), indicating that activation of bPAC mimics the activation of SACY by HCO3−.
evidence: This is inferred from the similarity of cAMP increases shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The presence of bPAC did not affect SACY expression level.
source: The presence of bPAC did not affect SACY expression level (Figure 2C), consistent with the observation that HCO3−-stimulated cAMP synthesis is similar in wild-type and bPAC sperm (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: HCO3−-stimulated cAMP synthesis is similar in wild-type and bPAC sperm.
source: The presence of bPAC did not affect SACY expression level (Figure 2C), consistent with the observation that HCO3−-stimulated cAMP synthesis is similar in wild-type and bPAC sperm (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is supported by cAMP measurements shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The expression level of PKA remained unchanged in bPAC sperm.
source: The expression level of PKA also remained unchanged in bPAC sperm (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The phosphorylation of PKA targets under non-stimulated conditions was not majorly different in bPAC sperm compared to wild-type sperm.
source: The phosphorylation of PKA targets under non-stimulated conditions was also not majorly different in bPAC sperm compared to wild-type sperm (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Stimulation of bPAC sperm with either light or HCO3− both evoked phosphorylation of PKA targets.
source: Furthermore, stimulation of bPAC sperm with either light or HCO3− both evoked phosphorylation of PKA targets (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Incubation with HCO3− or db-cAMP enhanced tyrosine phosphorylation to a similar extent in wild-type and bPAC sperm.
source: Finally, we analyzed whether the capacitation-associated phosphorylation of tyrosine residues was altered: incubation with HCO3− or the cAMP analog dibutyryl-cAMP (db-cAMP) enhanced tyrosine phosphorylation to a similar extent in wild-type and bPAC sperm (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: bPAC expression does not interfere with known cAMP-signaling events in sperm.
source: In summary, bPAC expression does not interfere with known cAMP-signaling events in sperm.
evidence: This is inferred from the data showing similar responses in wild-type and bPAC sperm.

claim: Under non-capacitating conditions in the dark, the percentage of sperm undergoing the acrosome reaction was similar between wild-type and bPAC sperm.
source: Under non-capacitating conditions (without HCO3−) in the dark, the percentage of sperm undergoing the acrosome reaction was similar between wild-type and bPAC sperm (wild-type: 34.1% versus bPAC: 41.7%; Figure 2F).
evidence: This is supported by acrosome reaction assay data shown in Figure 2F.

claim: After light-stimulation, the number of bPAC sperm undergoing the acrosome reaction increased dramatically.
source: After light-stimulation, the number of sperm undergoing the acrosome reaction changed dramatically for bPAC sperm but remained unchanged for wild-type sperm (wild-type: 38.4% bPAC: 70.5%; Figure 2F).
evidence: This is supported by acrosome reaction assay data shown in Figure 2F.

claim: After light-stimulation, the number of wild-type sperm undergoing the acrosome reaction remained unchanged.
source: After light-stimulation, the number of sperm undergoing the acrosome reaction changed dramatically for bPAC sperm but remained unchanged for wild-type sperm (wild-type: 38.4% bPAC: 70.5%; Figure 2F).
evidence: This is supported by acrosome reaction assay data shown in Figure 2F.

claim: A light-stimulated increase in cAMP levels results in sperm capacitation.
source: This demonstrates that a light-stimulated increase in cAMP levels results in sperm capacitation and that bPAC functionally mimics the activation of SACY by HCO3−.
evidence: This is inferred from the acrosome reaction data shown in Figure 2F.

claim: bPAC functionally mimics the activation of SACY by HCO3− in inducing capacitation.
source: This demonstrates that a light-stimulated increase in cAMP levels results in sperm capacitation and that bPAC functionally mimics the activation of SACY by HCO3−.
evidence: This is inferred from the acrosome reaction data shown in Figure 2F.

claim: In mammalian sperm, cAMP controls the flagellar beat.
source: In mammalian sperm, cAMP controls the flagellar beat (Wennemuth et al., 2003; Esposito et al., 2004; Nolan et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Wennemuth et al., 2003; Esposito et al., 2004; Nolan et al., 2004.

claim: The basal beat frequency of bPAC sperm was slightly lower compared to wild-type sperm.
source: The basal beat frequency of bPAC sperm was slightly lower compared to wild-type sperm (5.5 ± 2.5 Hz versus 8.0 ± 3.7 Hz; Figure 2G), which might be due to a cAMP-dependent feedback mechanism activated by elevated basal cAMP levels (Burton and McKnight, 2007).
evidence: This is supported by beat frequency measurements shown in Figure 2G.

claim: The lower basal beat frequency in bPAC sperm might be due to a cAMP-dependent feedback mechanism activated by elevated basal cAMP levels.
source: The basal beat frequency of bPAC sperm was slightly lower compared to wild-type sperm (5.5 ± 2.5 Hz versus 8.0 ± 3.7 Hz; Figure 2G), which might be due to a cAMP-dependent feedback mechanism activated by elevated basal cAMP levels (Burton and McKnight, 2007).
evidence: This is speculative reasoning supported by a citation to Burton and McKnight, 2007.

claim: A 200-ms light pulse increased the beat frequency of bPAC sperm within 10 s about 2.5-fold from 7 Hz to 18 Hz.
source: Light stimulation of bPAC sperm evoked a transient acceleration of the flagellar beat: a 200-ms light pulse increased the beat frequency within 10 s about 2.5-fold from 7 Hz to 18 Hz (Figure 2H; Videos 1,2).
evidence: This is supported by beat frequency measurements shown in Figure 2H and Videos 1,2.

claim: The acceleration of flagellar beat persisted for at least 10 s after light stimulation.
source: The acceleration persisted for at least 10 s and sperm returned to basal beat frequency within 30 s (Figure 2H).
evidence: This is supported by beat frequency measurements shown in Figure 2H.

claim: Sperm returned to basal beat frequency within 30 s after light stimulation.
source: The acceleration persisted for at least 10 s and sperm returned to basal beat frequency within 30 s (Figure 2H).
evidence: This is supported by beat frequency measurements shown in Figure 2H.

claim: The light-stimulated acceleration of the flagellar beat was dose-dependent.
source: The light-stimulated acceleration of the flagellar beat was dose-dependent: the longer the light exposure, the faster the onset and higher the beat frequency (Figure 2I,J).
evidence: This is supported by dose-response data shown in Figures 2I and 2J.

claim: The longer the light exposure, the faster the onset and higher the beat frequency.
source: The light-stimulated acceleration of the flagellar beat was dose-dependent: the longer the light exposure, the faster the onset and higher the beat frequency (Figure 2I,J).
evidence: This is supported by dose-response data shown in Figures 2I and 2J.

claim: Local illumination of a small part of the flagellum enhanced the beat frequency.
source: Local illumination of a small part of the flagellum also enhanced the beat frequency, albeit the increase was smaller and its kinetics slower compared to global illumination (Figure 2K, Videos 3,4).
evidence: This is supported by beat frequency measurements shown in Figure 2K and Videos 3,4.

claim: The increase in beat frequency from local illumination was smaller and its kinetics slower compared to global illumination.
source: Local illumination of a small part of the flagellum also enhanced the beat frequency, albeit the increase was smaller and its kinetics slower compared to global illumination (Figure 2K, Videos 3,4).
evidence: This is supported by beat frequency measurements shown in Figure 2K and Videos 3,4.

claim: Light activation of bPAC mimics the transient beat acceleration evoked by HCO3− stimulation of SACY.
source: Altogether, we conclude that (1) light activation of bPAC mimics the transient beat acceleration evoked by HCO3− stimulation of SACY (Wennemuth et al., 2003; Carlson et al., 2007), (2) the behavioral response of single cells can be modulated in a graded fashion, and that (3) bPAC is able to control cAMP signaling in the sperm flagellum with spatial precision.
evidence: This is inferred from the data and supported by citations to Wennemuth et al., 2003 and Carlson et al., 2007.

claim: The behavioral response of single cells can be modulated in a graded fashion using bPAC.
source: Altogether, we conclude that (1) light activation of bPAC mimics the transient beat acceleration evoked by HCO3− stimulation of SACY (Wennemuth et al., 2003; Carlson et al., 2007), (2) the behavioral response of single cells can be modulated in a graded fashion, and that (3) bPAC is able to control cAMP signaling in the sperm flagellum with spatial precision.
evidence: This is inferred from the dose-dependent responses shown in the data.

claim: bPAC is able to control cAMP signaling in the sperm flagellum with spatial precision.
source: Altogether, we conclude that (1) light activation of bPAC mimics the transient beat acceleration evoked by HCO3− stimulation of SACY (Wennemuth et al., 2003; Carlson et al., 2007), (2) the behavioral response of single cells can be modulated in a graded fashion, and that (3) bPAC is able to control cAMP signaling in the sperm flagellum with spatial precision.
evidence: This is inferred from the local illumination experiments shown in Figure 2K.

claim: cAMP synthesis via light stimulation of bPAC did not evoke a Ca2+ signal in mouse sperm.
source: We observed that cAMP synthesis via light stimulation of bPAC did not evoke a Ca2+ signal (Figure 3A–D), consistent with the observation that a HCO3−-induced cAMP increase does not affect [Ca2+]i in mouse (Wennemuth et al., 2003; Carlson et al., 2007) and human sperm (Strünker et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by Ca2+ measurements shown in Figures 3A-D.

claim: A HCO3−-induced cAMP increase does not affect [Ca2+]i in mouse sperm.
source: We observed that cAMP synthesis via light stimulation of bPAC did not evoke a Ca2+ signal (Figure 3A–D), consistent with the observation that a HCO3−-induced cAMP increase does not affect [Ca2+]i in mouse (Wennemuth et al., 2003; Carlson et al., 2007) and human sperm (Strünker et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Wennemuth et al., 2003 and Carlson et al., 2007.

claim: A HCO3−-induced cAMP increase does not affect [Ca2+]i in human sperm.
source: We observed that cAMP synthesis via light stimulation of bPAC did not evoke a Ca2+ signal (Figure 3A–D), consistent with the observation that a HCO3−-induced cAMP increase does not affect [Ca2+]i in mouse (Wennemuth et al., 2003; Carlson et al., 2007) and human sperm (Strünker et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Strünker et al., 2011.

claim: 8-Br-cAMP, 8-Br-cGMP, and db-cAMP evoked a Ca2+ signal in wild-type and bPAC sperm.
source: In contrast, 8-Br-cAMP, 8-Br-cGMP, and db-cAMP evoked a Ca2+ signal in wild-type and bPAC sperm (Figure 3A–C,E) that was abolished in CatSper-null sperm (Figure 3F); similar results have been reported by others (Ren et al., 2001; Xia et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by Ca2+ measurements shown in Figures 3A-C and 3E.

claim: The Ca2+ signal evoked by 8-Br-cAMP, 8-Br-cGMP, and db-cAMP was abolished in CatSper-null sperm.
source: In contrast, 8-Br-cAMP, 8-Br-cGMP, and db-cAMP evoked a Ca2+ signal in wild-type and bPAC sperm (Figure 3A–C,E) that was abolished in CatSper-null sperm (Figure 3F); similar results have been reported by others (Ren et al., 2001; Xia et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by Ca2+ measurements shown in Figure 3F.

claim: In human sperm, 8-Br-cNMPs directly activate CatSper via an extracellular site.
source: In human sperm, 8-Br-cNMPs directly activate CatSper via an extracellular site (Brenker et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Brenker et al., 2012.

claim: The loss of SACY function abolishes cAMP signaling in sperm, rendering sperm immotile and resulting in male infertility.
source: The loss of SACY function abolishes cAMP signaling in sperm, rendering sperm immotile and resulting in male infertility (Esposito et al., 2004; Xie et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Esposito et al., 2004 and Xie et al., 2006.

claim: Removal of extracellular Ca2+ attenuated HCO3−-induced cAMP synthesis by SACY.
source: Removal of extracellular Ca2+ attenuated HCO3−-induced cAMP synthesis by SACY (Figure 4A) (Jaiswal and Conti, 2003; Carlson et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by cAMP measurements shown in Figure 4A and citations to Jaiswal and Conti, 2003 and Carlson et al., 2007.

claim: Tyrosine phosphorylation in wild-type and bPAC sperm was largely abolished by removal of extracellular Ca2+.
source: Thereby, tyrosine phosphorylation in wild-type and bPAC sperm was largely abolished (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Elevation of basal cAMP levels by IBMX restored tyrosine phosphorylation in wild-type sperm in Ca2+-free medium.
source: Elevation of basal cAMP levels by the phosphodiesterase inhibitor IBMX restored tyrosine phosphorylation in wild-type sperm (Figure 4A,B).
evidence: This is supported by cAMP measurements and Western blot data shown in Figures 4A and 4B.

claim: In Ca2+-free medium, light-stimulated increase of cAMP levels restored tyrosine phosphorylation in bPAC sperm.
